statutes.act: Ipc As Both The Appellants Act

facts: The case is about two appellants, Sanjay and Narendra, who were convicted of murdering Roop Singh.
Roop Singh was the brother of Sheela, wife of one of the appellants, Sanjay.
According to the prosecution, Sanjay insisted his brother Roop Singh to sell his land to Narendra, which led to enmity between them.
On August 11, 1998, at 3:00 a.m., Roop Singh and Sheela were sleeping in their chowk when appellants-Narendra and Sanjay, along with another person, armed with tamancha (pistol), came to the house.
Appellant-Narendra fired multiple bullets at Roop Singh, causing bullet injuries on his head.
Sanjay fired at PW-2 Sheela, causing bullet injuries on her neck, abdomen, and right leg.
Roop Singh was taken to Safdarjung Hospital, Delhi, where he was operated and discharged in stable condition.
However, Roop Singh died 62 days after the incident due to septicaemia caused by the wounds sustained prior to his death.
issues: Whether the conviction of the appellants under Section 302 IPC is sustainable?
petitioner_arguments: The motive suggested by the prosecution is not a probable one.
Death of Roop Singh was due to septicaemia caused by lack of proper care after he was discharged from the hospital, and not directly caused by the appellants.
respondent_arguments: The intention to cause death can be inferred from the situs and nature of the injury and the weapon used.
The act was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
court_reasoning: The court drew inference that the injuries were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause the death, as seen in Jagtar Singh's case (1998 Indlaw SC 752) and Dhupa Chamar's case (2002 Indlaw SC 1636).
holding: The conviction of the appellants under Section 302 IPC is sustainable.
cases_cited: In Ganga Dass alias Godha vs. State of Haryana
and Dhupa Chamar And Ors. vs. State of Bihar
upon the judgment of this Court in Jagtar Singh And Anr. vs. State of Punjab
